questions.text: About how long does the Moon take to go through a complete cycle of phases, from one new moon to the next?
questions.solution: The cycle of lunar phases (a synodic month) lasts about 29.5 days
questions.hint: It is roughly a month

questions.text: What causes the seasons on Earth?

options: The tilt of the Earth's axis
The changing distance between the Earth and the Sun
feedback: The Earth is closest to the Sun in January, which is winter in the UK

questions.solution: The Earth's axis is tilted (about 23.5°), so each hemisphere gets more direct sunlight in its summer
questions.hint: The Earth is actually closest to the Sun in January

questions.text: What name is given to the phase of the Moon when the whole of the side facing Earth is lit? Give the name of the phase.

feedback.new moon: At new moon we see none of the lit side

questions.solution: At full moon the Moon is on the opposite side of the Earth from the Sun, so we see its whole lit side
questions.hint: The Moon is on the opposite side of the Earth from the Sun

questions.text: What type of eclipse happens when the Moon passes between the Sun and the Earth?

feedback: In a lunar eclipse the Earth is between the Sun and the Moon

questions.solution: In a solar eclipse the Moon blocks the Sun's light from part of the Earth
questions.hint: Which object is hidden from view?

questions.text: The gravity of which body mainly causes the tides on Earth? Give the name.

feedback.the Sun: The Sun has a smaller effect on the tides because it is so far away
feedback.Sun: The Sun has a smaller effect on the tides because it is so far away

questions.solution: The Moon's gravity pulls on the oceans, causing two tidal bulges
questions.hint: It is the closest large body to the Earth

questions.text: What are sunspots?

options: Cooler, darker regions on the Sun's surface
Hotter, brighter regions on the Sun's surface
Shadows of planets on the Sun

questions.solution: Sunspots are cooler areas of the photosphere, so they look darker
questions.hint: They look dark because they are cooler than the surrounding surface

questions.text: About how long does the Earth take to rotate once on its axis so that the Sun returns to the same position in the sky (a solar day)?
questions.solution: A solar day (noon to noon) is 24 hours
questions.hint: This is the length of an ordinary day

questions.text: What is a sidereal day?

options: The time for the Earth to rotate once relative to the distant stars, about 23 h 56 min
The time from one midday to the next, exactly 24 h
The time for the Moon to orbit the Earth
The time between two high tides
feedback: That is a solar day

questions.solution: A sidereal day is one rotation relative to the stars: about 23 hours 56 minutes
questions.hint: 'Sidereal' comes from the Latin for 'star'

questions.text: What name is given to the phase of the Moon when we cannot see any of its lit side? Give the name of the phase.

feedback.full moon: At full moon we see the whole lit side

questions.solution: At new moon the Moon is between the Earth and the Sun, so its lit side faces away from us
questions.hint: The Moon is between the Earth and the Sun

questions.text: What type of eclipse happens when the Earth passes between the Sun and the Moon?
questions.solution: In a lunar eclipse the Moon moves into the Earth's shadow
questions.hint: Which object goes into the shadow?

questions.text: What causes aurorae (the northern and southern lights)?

options: Charged particles from the Sun interacting with the Earth's magnetic field and atmosphere

questions.solution: Charged particles from the solar wind are guided by the magnetic field and make atoms in the upper atmosphere glow
questions.hint: They are linked to activity on the Sun

questions.text: How many high tides are there at most places on the coast in about one day?
questions.solution: There are two tidal bulges, so most places have two high tides a day (about every 12 h 25 min)
questions.hint: There is a tidal bulge on each side of the Earth

questions.text: Why do we always see the same side of the Moon from Earth?

options: The Moon rotates once on its axis in the same time as it takes to orbit the Earth
The Moon does not rotate at all
The Earth's shadow always hides the other side
The other side is always dark
feedback: The far side gets sunlight too — at new moon it is fully lit

questions.solution: The Moon's rotation period equals its orbital period (synchronous rotation)
questions.hint: Compare the Moon's rotation period with its orbital period

questions.text: In the northern hemisphere, which season is it when the North Pole is tilted towards the Sun? Give the season.

feedback.winter: In winter the northern hemisphere is tilted away from the Sun

questions.solution: When the North Pole tilts towards the Sun, the northern hemisphere gets more direct sunlight and longer days
questions.hint: Days are longest when your hemisphere tilts towards the Sun

questions.text: Why can a total solar eclipse only be seen from a small part of the Earth?

options: The darkest part of the Moon's shadow (the umbra) on the Earth is small
The Sun is too far away
Clouds block the view everywhere else

questions.solution: Only places inside the small umbra see a total eclipse; the larger penumbra sees a partial eclipse
questions.hint: Think about the size of the Moon's shadow on the Earth

questions.text: When do spring tides (the largest tidal range) happen?

options: When the Sun, Earth and Moon are in a line, at new moon and full moon
When the Sun and Moon are at right angles as seen from the Earth
When the Moon is furthest from the Earth
feedback: Spring tides happen about twice a month, all year round

questions.solution: When the Sun, Moon and Earth line up, their tidal effects add together, giving spring tides
questions.hint: Think about when the Sun's and Moon's pulls act in the same line

questions.text: A sidereal day is 23 hours 56 minutes. How many minutes is this in total? Give the number.
questions.solution: 23 × 60 = 1380 minutes, and 1380 + 56 = 1436 minutes
questions.hint: Convert the hours into minutes first

questions.text: At which phase must the Moon be for a lunar eclipse to happen?

feedback: At new moon the Moon is between the Sun and the Earth — that's when solar eclipses can happen

questions.solution: The Earth must be between the Sun and the Moon, so the Moon is full
questions.hint: The Earth must be between the Sun and the Moon

questions.text: Why is the Sun higher in the sky at midday in summer than in winter in the UK?

options: The northern hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun in summer
The Earth is closer to the Sun in summer
The Sun is bigger in summer
The Moon blocks the Sun in winter
feedback: The Earth is closest to the Sun in January

questions.solution: In June the northern hemisphere tilts towards the Sun, so the midday Sun is higher in the sky
questions.hint: Think about the tilt of the Earth's axis

questions.text: What is the name of the visible surface layer of the Sun? Give the name.

feedback.corona: The corona is the Sun's outer atmosphere, seen during a total eclipse

questions.solution: The photosphere is the visible surface of the Sun, where sunspots are seen
questions.hint: Its name contains the Greek word for 'light'

questions.text: Why do solar eclipses not happen every month?

options: The Moon's orbit is tilted relative to the Earth's orbit around the Sun
The Moon stops orbiting for some months
The Earth's orbit is a perfect circle

questions.solution: The Moon's orbit is tilted by about 5°, so at most new moons its shadow passes above or below the Earth
questions.hint: Think about whether the Sun, Moon and Earth line up exactly every month

questions.text: A thin crescent Moon is seen in the west just after sunset. Over the next week the lit part grows. What is happening?

options: The Moon is moving away from the Earth

questions.solution: A growing lit part means the Moon is waxing, towards first quarter and full moon
questions.hint: 'Waxing' means growing and 'waning' means shrinking

questions.text: The Earth is closest to the Sun in early January. Why is it winter in the UK then?

options: The northern hemisphere is tilted away from the Sun, so sunlight is spread out and days are short
The Sun gives out less energy in January
The Earth spins more slowly in winter

questions.solution: The tilt matters more than the distance: low Sun and short days mean less heating
questions.hint: Think about the tilt rather than the distance

questions.text: The Moon orbits the Earth in 27.3 days relative to the stars, but its phases repeat every 29.5 days. Give the term for the 29.5-day period.

feedback.sidereal month: The sidereal month is the 27.3-day orbit relative to the stars
feedback.sidereal: The sidereal month is the 27.3-day orbit relative to the stars

questions.solution: The 29.5-day cycle of phases is the synodic (lunar) month; the 27.3-day orbit is the sidereal month
questions.hint: It is measured relative to the Sun, not the stars

questions.text: What is an annular solar eclipse?

options: An eclipse in which the Moon is too far away to cover the Sun completely, leaving a ring of light
An eclipse of the Moon by the Earth's shadow
An eclipse that lasts for a whole day
An eclipse in which the Sun covers the Moon

questions.solution: When the Moon is near its furthest point it looks slightly smaller than the Sun, so a ring (annulus) is left
questions.hint: 'Annulus' means ring

questions.text: When do neap tides (the smallest tidal range) happen?

options: When the Sun and Moon are at right angles as seen from the Earth, at first and last quarter
When the Sun, Earth and Moon are in a straight line
When the Earth is closest to the Sun

questions.solution: At right angles, the Sun's tidal effect partly cancels the Moon's, giving neap tides
questions.hint: Compare with spring tides, when the effects add together

questions.text: Sunspots appear to move across the face of the Sun over several days. What does this show the Sun is doing? Give one word.
questions.solution: Sunspots move across the disc because the Sun rotates (about once every 25 to 30 days)
questions.hint: The spots are fixed to the Sun's surface

questions.text: During a total lunar eclipse the Moon often looks red. Why?

options: Sunlight is refracted through the Earth's atmosphere, and mostly red light reaches the Moon
The Moon gives out its own red light
Mars reflects red light onto it
The Moon is heated by the Sun until it glows

questions.solution: The atmosphere scatters blue light and bends (refracts) red light into the Earth's shadow
questions.hint: The light must pass through the Earth's atmosphere

questions.text: Why is a sidereal day shorter than a solar day?

options: The Earth moves along its orbit, so it must rotate a little further for the Sun to return to the same position
The Earth spins faster at night
The Moon slows the Earth down each day
The Sun moves around the Earth

questions.solution: In one day the Earth moves about 1° along its orbit, so it needs about 4 extra minutes of rotation to face the Sun again
questions.hint: Think about the Earth's movement along its orbit during one day

questions.text: Why are aurorae usually seen near the North and South Poles?

options: The Earth's magnetic field guides charged particles towards the poles
The poles are closer to the Sun
There is more ice there to reflect light

questions.solution: Charged particles follow the magnetic field lines, which come together near the magnetic poles
questions.hint: Think about the shape of the Earth's magnetic field

questions.text: The number of sunspots rises and falls in a regular cycle. About how long is this cycle?
questions.solution: The solar cycle of sunspot numbers lasts about 11 years
questions.hint: It is longer than a year but much shorter than a century

questions.text: At which phase of the Moon can a solar eclipse happen? Give the phase.

feedback.full moon: At full moon the Earth is between the Sun and the Moon — that's when a lunar eclipse can happen

questions.solution: The Moon must be between the Sun and the Earth, so it is at new moon
questions.hint: The Moon has to be between the Sun and the Earth

questions.text: Seen from the UK, the Sun rises in the north-east in June but in the south-east in December. Why?

options: The Earth's axis is tilted, so the Sun's apparent path across the sky changes through the year
The Sun moves across the galaxy
The Moon's gravity pulls the Sun

questions.solution: Because of the tilt, the Sun's declination changes during the year, changing where it rises
questions.hint: Think about how the tilt changes the Sun's path through the year

questions.text: Why is high tide about 50 minutes later each day?

options: The Moon moves along its orbit, so the Earth must turn a little further to face it again
The Earth slows down each day
The Sun moves further away each day
The oceans move more slowly at night

questions.solution: The Moon moves about 13° a day along its orbit, so the Earth needs about 50 extra minutes to face it again
questions.hint: Think about the Moon's movement during one day

questions.text: What is the name of the stream of charged particles that flows out from the Sun? Give the term.
questions.solution: The solar wind is a stream of charged particles from the Sun; it causes aurorae and pushes comet tails
questions.hint: It causes aurorae when it reaches the Earth

questions.text: Which planet is closest to the Sun?
questions.solution: The order from the Sun is Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune
questions.hint: Recall the order of the planets from the Sun

questions.text: Which is the largest planet in the Solar System?
questions.solution: Jupiter is the largest planet: its diameter is about 11 times the Earth's
questions.hint: It is a gas giant with a Great Red Spot

questions.text: Where is the main asteroid belt?
questions.solution: The main asteroid belt lies between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter
questions.hint: It separates the rocky planets from the gas giants

questions.text: Which dwarf planet was classed as the ninth planet until 2006? Give the name.
questions.solution: Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006
questions.hint: It is in the Kuiper belt, beyond Neptune

questions.text: What is a meteor?

options: A streak of light caused by a small piece of rock or dust burning up in the atmosphere
A rock from space that has landed on the ground
feedback: That is a meteorite

questions.solution: A meteor ('shooting star') is the glowing trail of a meteoroid burning up in the atmosphere
questions.hint: People sometimes call it a shooting star

questions.text: How many planets are there in the Solar System?

feedback: Pluto is no longer counted as a planet

questions.solution: There are eight planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune
questions.hint: Pluto is now a dwarf planet

questions.text: Which planet is often called the Red Planet? Give the name.
questions.solution: Mars looks red because its surface contains iron oxide
questions.hint: It is the fourth planet from the Sun

questions.text: Which planets are the rocky (terrestrial) planets?
questions.solution: The four inner planets are rocky; the four outer planets are giants
questions.hint: The rocky planets are the ones closest to the Sun

questions.text: What is a piece of rock from space that survives its fall and lands on the Earth's surface called? Give the term.

feedback.meteor: A meteor is the streak of light — the rock that reaches the ground has a different name
feedback.meteoroid: A meteoroid is the rock while it is still in space

questions.solution: A meteorite is a meteoroid that reaches the ground
questions.hint: It is not the streak of light in the sky

questions.text: Which statement describes a dwarf planet?

options: It orbits the Sun and is roughly round, but has not cleared its orbit of other objects
It is a moon that orbits a planet
It is any rock in the asteroid belt
It is a planet with no moons

questions.solution: A dwarf planet orbits the Sun and is round, but has not cleared the area around its orbit
questions.hint: Compare it with the definition of a planet

questions.text: Which way does a comet's tail point?

options: Always behind the comet along its path

questions.solution: The solar wind and radiation push the gas and dust away from the Sun
questions.hint: Think about what pushes the tail

questions.text: Which planet has the brightest and most obvious ring system? Give the name.

feedback.Jupiter: Jupiter has faint rings, but they are hard to see

questions.solution: Saturn's bright rings are made of ice and rock
questions.hint: It is the sixth planet from the Sun

questions.text: Which planet has a surface hot enough to melt lead, because its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat?

feedback: Mercury is closer to the Sun but has almost no atmosphere to trap heat

questions.solution: Venus has a runaway greenhouse effect, making it the hottest planet even though Mercury is closer to the Sun
questions.hint: It is not the planet closest to the Sun

questions.text: Which object is the largest in the asteroid belt and is classed as a dwarf planet?

feedback: Pluto is beyond Neptune, in the Kuiper belt

questions.solution: Ceres is the largest object in the asteroid belt and is a dwarf planet
questions.hint: Pluto and Eris are much further away, beyond Neptune

questions.text: Why does Mercury have a very large range of surface temperatures?

options: It has almost no atmosphere to trap heat
It has a thick cloud layer

questions.solution: With almost no atmosphere, the sunlit side gets very hot and the night side very cold
questions.hint: What would normally keep heat in at night?

questions.text: Which force keeps the planets in their orbits around the Sun? Give the name of the force.
questions.solution: The Sun's gravity provides the force that keeps the planets in orbit
questions.hint: It acts between any two masses

questions.text: What causes a meteor shower?

options: The Earth passing through a trail of dust left by a comet
The Earth passing through the asteroid belt
The Moon's shadow falling on the Earth

questions.solution: Comets leave dust trails; when the Earth crosses one, many meteors appear from the same direction
questions.hint: Meteor showers happen on about the same dates each year

questions.text: Which planet takes the longest time to orbit the Sun?
questions.solution: Neptune is the furthest planet from the Sun, so it has the longest orbital period (about 165 years)
questions.hint: The further a planet is from the Sun, the longer its year

questions.text: What is the name of the region of icy objects beyond Neptune that includes Pluto? Give the name.

feedback.Oort cloud: The Oort cloud is much further out and surrounds the whole Solar System
feedback.asteroid belt: The asteroid belt is between Mars and Jupiter

questions.solution: The Kuiper belt is a ring of icy bodies beyond Neptune, including Pluto
questions.hint: It is a flattened ring of icy bodies just beyond the orbit of Neptune

questions.text: Why does a comet grow a tail as it gets close to the Sun?

options: Heat from the Sun turns ice into gas, which is pushed away by the solar wind and radiation
The comet speeds up and stretches
The Sun's gravity pulls rock off the comet
The tail freezes onto the comet

questions.solution: Near the Sun, ice sublimes into gas and releases dust, which the solar wind and radiation push into tails
questions.hint: What happens to ice when it is heated?

questions.text: Which planet has the shortest orbital period? Give the name.
questions.solution: Mercury is closest to the Sun, so it has the shortest year (about 88 days)
questions.hint: The closer a planet is to the Sun, the shorter its year

questions.text: Which statement about the planets is correct?

options: The further a planet is from the Sun, the longer its orbital period
Planets further from the Sun orbit faster
All planets have the same orbital period
The inner planets have the longest years

questions.solution: Orbital period increases with distance from the Sun (Kepler's third law)
questions.hint: Compare Mercury's year (88 days) with Neptune's (about 165 years)

questions.text: Why are the inner planets rocky while the outer planets are mainly gas and ice?

options: Near the young Sun it was too hot for ices to form, so only rock and metal became solid
The outer planets formed much later
The Sun's gravity pulled the gas inwards
The rocky planets lost their gas to the Moon

questions.solution: Close to the young Sun only rock and metal could condense; further out ices formed too and planets grew large enough to hold gas
questions.hint: Think about temperature at different distances from the young Sun

questions.text: A space probe that goes into orbit around a planet is called an orbiter. What do we call a probe that passes close to a planet without stopping? Give the term.
questions.solution: A flyby probe passes a planet once, collecting data as it goes past
questions.hint: It flies past the planet

questions.text: What advantage does a lander have over an orbiter?

options: It can study the surface directly and analyse samples
It can map the whole planet

questions.solution: A lander can make close-up measurements of the surface and analyse rocks and soil
questions.hint: Think about what you can only do on the surface

questions.text: Which idea about the Moon's origin is supported by most scientists?

options: It formed from debris after a Mars-sized body collided with the early Earth
It was captured by the Earth's gravity as it passed by
It split off from a fast-spinning Earth

questions.solution: The giant impact hypothesis explains the Moon's composition, which is similar to the Earth's mantle
questions.hint: The Moon's rocks are very similar to the Earth's mantle

questions.text: What is the name of the very distant, spherical cloud of icy objects thought to be the source of long-period comets? Give the name.

feedback.Kuiper belt: The Kuiper belt is closer, just beyond Neptune, and is a flattened ring

questions.solution: The Oort cloud surrounds the Solar System far beyond the Kuiper belt
questions.hint: It is thought to surround the whole Solar System, far beyond Pluto

questions.text: Why does Venus appear so bright in the night sky?

options: It is close to the Earth and its thick clouds reflect a lot of sunlight

questions.solution: Venus is close to us and its bright clouds reflect most of the sunlight that hits them
questions.hint: Planets do not produce their own light

questions.text: According to the nebular hypothesis, how did the Solar System form?

options: A cloud of gas and dust collapsed under gravity, forming the Sun and a disc in which the planets formed
The planets formed first and the Sun formed later
A star exploded and its pieces became the planets
The Sun captured planets from other stars

questions.solution: A collapsing nebula spun into a disc; the Sun formed at the centre and the planets formed from the disc
questions.hint: Think about what gravity does to a cloud of gas and dust

questions.text: Why can a probe land on the surface of Mars but not on the surface of Jupiter?

options: Jupiter is a gas giant with no solid surface
Jupiter is too cold for probes

questions.solution: Jupiter is made mostly of hydrogen and helium with no solid surface to land on
questions.hint: Think about what Jupiter is mostly made of

questions.text: Comets with very elongated orbits are bright for only a short part of each orbit. Why?

options: They are only close enough to the Sun to grow bright tails for a small part of their orbit
They stop moving for most of their orbit
The Moon hides them for most of their orbit

questions.solution: Far from the Sun the nucleus is frozen and dark; only near the Sun does it release gas and dust
questions.hint: Where in its orbit does a comet grow a tail?

questions.text: Which evidence suggests that Mars once had liquid water on its surface?

options: Dried-up river channels and minerals that form in water

questions.solution: Orbiters and rovers have found ancient river channels and minerals that only form in water
questions.hint: Look for evidence that water shaped the surface

questions.text: We can see planets in the night sky even though they do not produce their own light. What do they do to sunlight that lets us see them? Give one word.
questions.solution: Planets do not produce light; they reflect sunlight towards us
questions.hint: Think about how the Moon is lit up

questions.text: Why is Pluto no longer classed as a planet?

options: It has not cleared the area around its orbit of other objects
It is too far from the Sun
feedback: Pluto has several moons, including Charon

questions.solution: Pluto shares its region with many Kuiper belt objects, so it has not cleared its orbit
questions.hint: Think about the three conditions for being a planet

questions.text: Why does the Earth have far fewer visible impact craters than the Moon?

options: Weathering, erosion and plate movements on the Earth have removed most old craters
Far fewer objects have ever hit the Earth
The Earth's gravity is weaker than the Moon's
The Moon is closer to the asteroid belt
feedback: The Earth is a bigger target with stronger gravity, so it has been hit at least as often
The Earth's gravity is stronger than the Moon's

questions.solution: Both were hit many times, but on the Earth weathering, erosion and moving plates have destroyed most craters
questions.hint: Think about how wind, water and moving plates change the Earth's surface over time

questions.text: What is the name of our galaxy?

feedback: Andromeda is the nearest large galaxy to ours
Orion is a constellation

questions.solution: Our Solar System is in the Milky Way galaxy
questions.hint: It appears as a faint band of light across a dark sky

questions.text: Which process releases energy in the core of a star like the Sun?

feedback: Fission splits large nuclei — stars join small nuclei together

questions.solution: Hydrogen nuclei fuse to form helium in the core, releasing energy
questions.hint: Small nuclei join together

questions.text: What is a cloud of gas and dust in space in which stars form called? Give the term.
questions.solution: Stars form when gravity pulls together the gas and dust of a nebula
questions.hint: Its name comes from the Latin word for mist or cloud

questions.text: What will the Sun be at the very end of its life?

feedback: Only very massive stars can form black holes
The Sun is not massive enough to become a supernova

questions.solution: The Sun will become a red giant, then lose its outer layers and end as a white dwarf
questions.hint: The Sun is not massive enough to explode

questions.text: What is the name of the theory that the universe began from a very small, hot, dense state about 13.8 billion years ago? Give the name.
questions.solution: The Big Bang theory says the universe began very small, hot and dense and has been expanding ever since
questions.hint: The universe has been expanding ever since

questions.text: What is a planet that orbits a star other than the Sun called?
questions.solution: Exoplanets orbit other stars; thousands have been discovered
questions.hint: 'Exo' means 'outside'

questions.text: Which colour are the hottest stars?

feedback: Red stars are the coolest

questions.solution: Hotter stars emit more short-wavelength light, so the hottest stars look blue
questions.hint: Think about the colour of the hottest part of a flame

questions.text: What is a light year?

options: The distance light travels in one year
The time light takes to reach the Earth from the Sun
The time the Earth takes to orbit the Sun

questions.solution: A light year is a distance: about 9.5 × 10^12 km
questions.hint: It is a unit of distance, not time

questions.text: What is the name of the huge explosion at the end of the life of a massive star? Give the term.
questions.solution: A massive star ends its life in a supernova explosion
questions.hint: It can briefly outshine a whole galaxy

questions.text: A main sequence star like the Sun runs out of hydrogen in its core. Which stage comes next?
questions.solution: The star swells into a red giant
questions.hint: The star expands and its surface cools

questions.text: What is redshift?

options: An increase in the wavelength of light from an object moving away from us
A decrease in the wavelength of light from an object moving towards us
The colour of the Sun at sunset
feedback: That is blueshift

questions.solution: Light from a receding object is stretched to longer wavelengths, towards the red end of the spectrum
questions.hint: Wavelength is stretched when the source moves away

questions.text: What type of galaxy is the Milky Way? Give the type.
questions.solution: The Milky Way is a (barred) spiral galaxy
questions.hint: It has arms that wind out from the centre

questions.text: During which stage do stars spend most of their lives?
questions.solution: Stars spend about 90% of their lives on the main sequence, fusing hydrogen into helium
questions.hint: This is the stable stage when hydrogen is fused in the core

questions.text: Which element is fused into helium in the core of a main sequence star? Give the name.

feedback.helium: Helium is the product of the fusion — name the element that is fused

questions.solution: Main sequence stars fuse hydrogen nuclei into helium
questions.hint: It is the lightest element

questions.text: A star is 4.2 light years away. What does this tell you about the light we see from it?

options: It left the star about 4.2 years ago
It left the star 4.2 days ago
The star is 4.2 times bigger than the Sun

questions.solution: Light takes one year to travel one light year, so we see the star as it was 4.2 years ago
questions.hint: A light year is the distance light travels in one year

questions.text: Light from a distant galaxy shows a large redshift. What does this tell us?

options: The galaxy is moving away from us quickly
The galaxy is moving towards us

questions.solution: A large redshift means a large recession speed
questions.hint: What does a stretched wavelength tell you about movement?

questions.text: What is the name of a region where gravity is so strong that not even light can escape? Give the term.
questions.solution: A black hole can form from the core left after a very massive star explodes
questions.hint: It can form after a very massive star explodes

questions.text: On a Hertzsprung–Russell (HR) diagram, where are white dwarfs found?

feedback: Top right is where red giants and supergiants are

questions.solution: White dwarfs are hot (left of the diagram) but small, so they have low luminosity (bottom)
questions.hint: Temperature increases to the left on an HR diagram; luminosity increases upwards

questions.text: Which observation is evidence for the Big Bang?
questions.solution: The cosmic microwave background is radiation left over from the hot early universe
questions.hint: It is radiation found in every direction in space

questions.text: Gravity pulls gas and dust together to form a very young star before nuclear fusion starts. What is it called? Give the term.
questions.solution: A protostar heats up as it collapses; when fusion starts it becomes a main sequence star
questions.hint: Its name starts with a Greek word meaning 'first'

questions.text: Which method has found many exoplanets by detecting a small, regular dip in a star's brightness?
questions.solution: When a planet passes in front of its star, the star's brightness dips slightly
questions.hint: The planet passes in front of its star

questions.text: Star X has a parallax angle of 0.5 arcseconds and star Y has a parallax angle of 0.1 arcseconds. Which statement is correct?

options: Star Y is further away than star X
Star X is further away than star Y
Both stars are the same distance away
Parallax angle does not depend on distance

questions.solution: Distance = 1 ÷ parallax: star X is 2 pc away and star Y is 10 pc away
questions.hint: A smaller parallax angle means a greater distance

questions.text: Why does a main sequence star like the Sun not collapse under its own gravity?

options: Outward pressure from the energy released by fusion balances the inward pull of gravity

questions.solution: The star is stable because the outward pressure from fusion balances gravity
questions.hint: Two forces are in balance

questions.text: A line in the spectrum of a galaxy has a wavelength of 660 nm. In a laboratory the same line is at 600 nm. Is the galaxy moving towards us or away from us? Answer towards or away.

feedback.towards: Moving towards us would make the wavelength shorter — here it is longer

questions.solution: The wavelength is longer (redshifted), so the galaxy is moving away from us
questions.hint: Is the observed wavelength longer or shorter than in the laboratory?

questions.text: Two stars look equally bright from Earth, but star X is further away than star Y. What can you conclude?

options: Star X gives out more light (is more luminous) than star Y
Star Y is more luminous than star X
The two stars are equally luminous
Star X must be cooler than star Y

questions.solution: To look as bright from further away, star X must give out more light
questions.hint: Light gets fainter with distance

questions.text: What did Edwin Hubble find about distant galaxies?

options: The further away a galaxy is, the faster it is moving away from us
Nearby galaxies are moving away fastest
All galaxies are moving towards us

questions.solution: Hubble found that recession speed is proportional to distance, which is evidence for an expanding universe
questions.hint: Compare the redshift of near and far galaxies

questions.text: Where are elements heavier than iron made?

options: In the core of main sequence stars like the Sun

questions.solution: Fusion in normal stars stops at iron; heavier elements are made in the extreme conditions of a supernova
questions.hint: Fusion in normal stars stops at iron

questions.text: Why do massive stars have much shorter lives than stars like the Sun?

options: They use up their hydrogen much faster
They are further from the Earth
feedback: Massive stars contain more hydrogen, but they use it up much faster

questions.solution: Massive stars have more fuel, but their much higher core temperatures make them fuse it far faster
questions.hint: Think about how fast they fuse their fuel

questions.text: Why do scientists think that the universe is expanding?

options: Light from distant galaxies is redshifted, and more distant galaxies show a greater redshift
The Milky Way is getting brighter
The Sun is moving away from the Earth

questions.solution: Redshift increasing with distance shows that space itself is expanding
questions.hint: What does the redshift of galaxies show?

questions.text: Why does the parallax method only work for relatively nearby stars?

options: For distant stars the parallax angle is too small to measure accurately

questions.solution: Parallax angles get smaller with distance; for distant stars they are too small to measure
questions.hint: How does the parallax angle change as distance increases?

questions.text: What is the cosmic microwave background radiation thought to be?

options: Radiation left over from the hot early universe, now stretched to microwave wavelengths
Microwaves given out by the Sun

questions.solution: It is radiation from the early universe whose wavelength has been stretched as the universe expanded
questions.hint: Think about what happens to the wavelength of radiation as the universe expands

questions.text: A star like the Sun throws off its outer layers as a planetary nebula. What is the hot, dense core that is left behind called? Give the term.

feedback.red dwarf: A red dwarf is a small, cool main sequence star
feedback.red giant: The red giant is the stage before the outer layers are thrown off

questions.solution: The exposed core is a white dwarf, which slowly cools
questions.hint: It is small, hot and dim

questions.text: A line in the spectrum of a nearby star has a slightly shorter wavelength than in the laboratory. What does this show?

options: The star is moving towards us
The star is moving away from us
The star is a black hole

questions.solution: A shorter wavelength is a blueshift, so the star is moving towards us
questions.hint: Is this a redshift or a blueshift?

questions.text: What is the name for how bright a star would appear if it were 10 parsecs from the Earth? Give the term.

feedback.apparent magnitude: Apparent magnitude is how bright a star looks from Earth at its real distance

questions.solution: Absolute magnitude compares the true brightness of stars by imagining them all 10 pc away
questions.hint: It lets astronomers compare stars fairly

questions.text: A star's light shows that it is moving away from us. Which word describes the shift in the wavelength of its light? Give the term.

feedback.blueshift: A blueshift happens when the source moves towards us

questions.solution: A source moving away has its light stretched to longer wavelengths: a redshift
questions.hint: The wavelengths are stretched

questions.text: What does a refracting telescope use to collect and focus light?

feedback: Mirrors are used in reflecting telescopes

questions.solution: A refracting telescope uses lenses to bend (refract) light
questions.hint: 'Refract' means to bend light as it passes through glass

questions.text: What does a reflecting telescope use to collect and focus light?

feedback: Lenses are used in refracting telescopes

questions.solution: A reflecting telescope uses a curved (concave) mirror
questions.hint: 'Reflect' gives you a clue

questions.text: The sky is divided into 88 official regions. What is each region called? Give the term.
questions.solution: The sky is divided into 88 constellations, such as Orion and Ursa Major
questions.hint: Orion is an example of one

questions.text: What causes light pollution?

options: Artificial lights such as street lights

questions.solution: Artificial light scattered by the atmosphere brightens the sky, hiding faint stars
questions.hint: It is a problem near towns and cities

questions.text: Which type of telescope is used to detect radio waves from space?

options: A radio telescope, usually a large dish

questions.solution: Radio telescopes use large dishes to collect radio waves
questions.hint: Radio waves are not visible light

questions.text: What is the name of the star that stays almost fixed in the sky above the Earth's North Pole? Give the name.
questions.solution: Polaris (the Pole Star) is very close to the north celestial pole
questions.hint: It is used to find the direction of north at night

questions.text: Why are many observatories built on high mountains?

options: There is less atmosphere above them to blur and absorb light
They are closer to the stars
feedback: The extra height is tiny compared with the distance to the stars

questions.solution: High sites have thinner, drier air above them and less light pollution
questions.hint: Think about how much air the light has to pass through

questions.text: What is declination?

options: The angle of an object north or south of the celestial equator
The angle east of the meridian

questions.solution: Declination is like latitude on the sky, measured in degrees from the celestial equator
questions.hint: It is the sky's version of latitude

questions.text: What is the name of the imaginary sphere around the Earth on which the stars appear to lie? Give the term.
questions.solution: Astronomers imagine the stars on a celestial sphere around the Earth
questions.hint: 'Celestial' means 'of the sky'

questions.text: Which sky coordinate is the equivalent of longitude on Earth?

feedback: Declination is the sky's equivalent of latitude

questions.solution: Right ascension (RA) is like longitude; declination is like latitude
questions.hint: Declination is the equivalent of latitude

questions.text: Why can telescopes in space produce sharper images than telescopes on the ground?

options: They are above the atmosphere, which blurs and absorbs light
They are closer to the stars

questions.solution: Above the atmosphere there is no blurring by moving air and no absorption
questions.hint: What does the light from a star pass through before it reaches a ground telescope?

questions.text: What is the name for the point in the sky directly above an observer? Give the term.
questions.solution: The zenith is the point directly overhead
questions.hint: It is at an altitude of 90°

questions.text: Why do the stars appear to move across the sky during the night?

options: The Earth rotates on its axis
The Earth orbits the Sun once a night

questions.solution: The Earth spins once a day, so the stars appear to move from east to west
questions.hint: Something is turning — is it the Earth or the sky?

questions.text: Why can a telescope with a larger aperture show fainter objects?
questions.solution: A larger aperture has a larger collecting area, so it gathers more light from faint objects
questions.hint: Think about the area of the lens or mirror

questions.text: Which parts of the electromagnetic spectrum from space reach the ground without being absorbed much by the atmosphere?
questions.solution: The atmosphere has 'windows' for visible light and radio waves; it absorbs X-rays, gamma rays and most UV
questions.hint: Ground-based observatories mainly use two types of telescope

questions.text: An astronomer wants to observe X-rays from a black hole. Where must the telescope be?

options: In space, because the atmosphere absorbs X-rays

questions.solution: X-rays are absorbed by the atmosphere, so X-ray telescopes must be in space
questions.hint: Do X-rays from space reach the ground?

questions.text: Polaris has a declination of almost +90°. Which point in the sky is it close to? Give the term.
questions.solution: A declination of +90° is the north celestial pole, directly above the Earth's North Pole
questions.hint: Declination is measured from the celestial equator (0°)

questions.text: Why is it easier to see faint stars in the countryside than in a city?

options: There are more stars above the countryside

questions.solution: Without bright artificial lights, the sky is darker and faint stars can be seen
questions.hint: What makes the sky bright at night in a city?

questions.text: In astronomy, what is the meridian?

options: An imaginary line across the sky from north to south, through the zenith
A line around the celestial equator

questions.solution: Objects reach their highest point in the sky when they cross the meridian
questions.hint: Objects are highest in the sky when they cross it

questions.text: Which instrument splits light from a star into its different wavelengths?
questions.solution: A spectroscope uses a prism or diffraction grating to form a spectrum
questions.hint: Its name is linked to the word 'spectrum'

questions.text: What is a planisphere used for?

options: Finding which stars and constellations are visible at a given date and time
Measuring the temperature of a star

questions.solution: A planisphere is a rotating star map: you set the date and time to see what is visible
questions.hint: It is a kind of star map

questions.text: Why can radio telescopes be used in daytime and in cloudy weather?

options: Radio waves pass through clouds, and daylight does not interfere with them
Radio waves are brighter than light
Radio waves travel faster than light
Clouds reflect radio waves towards the dish

questions.solution: Clouds do not block radio waves, and scattered sunlight is visible light, so it does not swamp radio signals
questions.hint: Think about what clouds and daylight affect

questions.text: Why are radio telescope dishes much larger than the mirrors of optical telescopes?

options: Radio waves have much longer wavelengths, so a large dish is needed to see detail
Radio sources are closer to the Earth

questions.solution: Resolution depends on wavelength ÷ diameter, so long radio waves need very large dishes
questions.hint: Compare the wavelengths of radio waves and visible light

questions.text: Polaris is almost at the north celestial pole. From a place at latitude 52° N, what is the approximate altitude of Polaris above the northern horizon, in degrees? Give the number.
questions.solution: The altitude of the north celestial pole equals the observer's latitude: about 52°
questions.hint: Compare the altitude of the pole star with your latitude

questions.text: A star has a declination of −70°. Why can it never be seen from the UK (latitude about 52° N)?

options: It never rises above the UK's horizon, because it is too far south
It is always hidden behind Polaris

questions.solution: From latitude 52° N, stars south of declination −38° never rise above the horizon
questions.hint: Think about how far south in the sky you can see from the UK

questions.text: Which problem do refracting telescopes have that reflecting telescopes avoid?

options: Lenses split white light into colours, causing coloured fringes (chromatic aberration)

questions.solution: Lenses refract different colours by different amounts; mirrors reflect all colours equally
questions.hint: Glass bends different colours by different amounts

questions.text: Which constellation contains the seven bright stars of the Plough (the Big Dipper)? Give the name.

feedback.Ursa Minor: Ursa Minor (the Little Bear) contains Polaris

questions.solution: The Plough is an asterism within Ursa Major, the Great Bear
questions.hint: Its English name is a large animal

questions.text: What is a circumpolar star?

options: A star that never sets below the horizon from a given place
A star that orbits the Pole Star
A star on the celestial equator
A star that can only be seen from the poles

questions.solution: Circumpolar stars are close enough to the celestial pole that they circle it without setting
questions.hint: Think about stars near the celestial pole

questions.text: How does a larger aperture affect the detail a telescope can show, for the same wavelength of light?

options: It improves the resolution, so finer detail can be seen
It has no effect on detail
It only changes the colour of the image

questions.solution: Resolution improves as aperture increases, so a larger telescope can separate objects that are closer together
questions.hint: Resolution depends on wavelength and aperture

questions.text: Why do astronomers combine signals from several radio dishes that are far apart?

options: Together they act like one huge dish, giving much better resolution
It makes the radio waves stronger
It makes the dishes cheaper to build

questions.solution: Interferometry: dishes far apart act like a single dish as wide as their separation
questions.hint: Think about how resolution depends on the size of the dish

questions.text: Why do stars twinkle when seen from the ground?

options: Moving air in the atmosphere bends their light by changing amounts
The stars change brightness every second
The stars are moving very fast

questions.solution: Turbulence in the atmosphere makes the starlight refract by changing amounts
questions.hint: Space telescopes do not see twinkling

questions.text: What is the name of the line in the sky that is the projection of the Earth's equator onto the celestial sphere? Give the term.

feedback.ecliptic: The ecliptic is the Sun's apparent yearly path, which is tilted to this line

questions.solution: The celestial equator is at declination 0°
questions.hint: It is at declination 0°

questions.text: A telescope has an objective lens of focal length 1000 mm and an eyepiece of focal length 25 mm. What is its magnification?

feedback: Divide the focal lengths — don't add them

questions.solution: Magnification = focal length of objective ÷ focal length of eyepiece = 1000 ÷ 25 = 40
questions.hint: Divide one focal length by the other

questions.text: Why are some infrared and ultraviolet telescopes placed in space?

options: Much infrared and ultraviolet radiation is absorbed by the atmosphere
These waves travel too slowly through air
These sources are very close to the Earth

questions.solution: Water vapour absorbs much infrared and the ozone layer absorbs ultraviolet, so space telescopes are needed
questions.hint: Think about what the atmosphere absorbs

questions.text: Which scientist first used a telescope to observe Jupiter's four largest moons, in 1610? Give the surname.

feedback.Newton: Newton built the first practical reflecting telescope in 1668

questions.solution: Galileo Galilei discovered Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto in 1610
questions.hint: He was an Italian scientist who also studied falling objects
